Current pipelines use model-free reinforcement learning, either merging per-motion specialists through lossy distillation, or brute-forcing a single policy with cluster-scale compute. SuperMimic amortizes learning across all motions with one differentiable world model of their shared dynamics, fit from logged transitions of a standard rigid-body simulator. The world model and the tracking policy train together in one loop, and backpropagation-through-time over short imagined rollouts gives the policy analytic gradients. Fast imagined rollouts and analytic gradients make policy learning efficient. In 3 hours on a single GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the return of a state-of-the-art motion tracker baseline trained for 7 days on 128 GPUs. It reduces GPU-hours by more than $1000\times$ and fails on only 25 of 129,514 benchmark motions, versus 179 failures for the baseline. After 9.8 hours on two GPUs, SuperMimic achieves zero failures. From 1 to 264 hours of motion, the world model's prediction error stays stable, and GPU-hours to a target return grow slowly. Our policy transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions. SuperMimic removes compute as the bottleneck to scaling humanoid whole-body control, making it practical to measure motion-tracking scaling laws.

papers.title: Interior $C^2$ Estimates and a Liouville Theorem for the Complex Monge-Ampère Equation under a Quadratic Lower Bound
papers.abstract: Let $n\ge2$ and let $u$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic Bedford-Taylor solution of the complex Monge-Ampère equation $\det(u_{i\bar j})=f$. Assume that in a sufficiently large ball centered at the origin in $\mathbb{C}^{n}$ \[ u(z)\ge δ\sum_{i=1}^{n}|x_i|^2,\qquad x_i=\operatorname{Re}z_{i},\qquad δ>0, \] and $u(0)\leq H$. If $f$ is Dini-continuous, bounded above and bounded away from zero, and satisfies $Δ_{\mathbb {R}}(f^{1/n})\ge-K$ in distributions, we derive an interior bound for the real $C^{2}$ norm on the unit ball $B_{1}(0)$. When $f\equiv1$, every entire solution satisfying $u(z)\geδ\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\operatorname{Re}z_i|^2$ for all $z\in\mathbb{C}^{n}$ and some $δ>0$ is a real quadratic polynomial.

papers.title: The T-matrix method for modeling the optical properties of grains in exoplanetary atmospheres
papers.abstract: Observations of exoplanetary atmospheres have revealed a rather complex co-existence between the gaseous and condensed phases, ranging from atmospheres apparently covered in clouds to clear ones, across a myriad of intermediate regimes. The interaction between solids and stellar radiation is of fundamental importance when forward or retrieval models are compared to observations. The simplest approach is to assume spherical particles, whose scattering and absorption properties are readily computed with Mie theory. More advanced computational methods, however, can also treat non-spherical condensates. Among these, the transition matrix approach has proven to provide a rigorous and efficient calculation of the extinction by non-spherical particles over a broad range of sizes and refractive indices. We here focus on the absorption and scattering cross sections of forsterite, spinel and silicon monoxide from the near to the far infrared range for particles of different sizes, with shapes ranging from compact ensembles of spheres to porous aggregates. We find that, depending on the size and the configuration chosen, the differences in extinction can be as high as a factor of 2-3, with structured grains being more efficient absorbers in the near infrared for sizes greater than 1 $μ$m. In a fiducial transmission spectrum we show that in the $λ= 1-5\,μ$m range the amount of spherical material needed to match the contribution of the structured grains can be a factor 2 higher. Such calculations, available for the community through a Zenodo repository, prove to be useful for interpreting recent and future observations of exoplanetary atmospheres.

papers.title: A Polynomial Criterion for Adaptive Stabilization of Discrete-Time Stochastic Nonlinear Systems with an Unknown Input Gain
papers.abstract: We consider scalar discrete-time systems whose nonlinear function is a linear combination of known power functions with unknown coefficients. The input gain is nonzero and unknown, and the noise is iid zero-mean Gaussian with unknown positive variance. We show that global stabilizability is equivalent to the joint positivity of a family of polynomials determined solely by the power exponents. When this condition holds, a feedback law depending only on the exponents makes the average squared output converge almost surely to the noise variance, the smallest possible value. When the condition fails, every Borel feedback law yields divergence of the output magnitude with positive probability for some fixed parameters and a deterministic initial state.

papers.title: Entropic metastability for drifted reflected Brownian motion: quasi-stationary distributions, regularity, and the exit position distribution
papers.abstract: Motivated by entropic metastability and the narrow escape problem, we investigate quasi-stationary distributions for reflected, drifted elliptic diffusions under mixed absorbing-reflecting boundary conditions on a bounded domain. We address two problems, which are solved completely independently of each other. First, using purely probabilistic tools, we prove the existence and uniqueness of a quasi-stationary distribution under minimal regularity assumptions on the coefficients (the case of an unbounded domain is also analyzed). Second, using spectral theory and the theory of strongly continuous semigroups on L p spaces, we study the analytical properties of the quasistationary distribution. We relate it to the principal eigenfunction of the adjoint of the associated (non-symmetric) infinitesimal generator with mixed absorbing-reflecting boundary conditions, and we establish its regularity up to the interface between the two boundary parts. We also fully characterize the law of the exit point when the process is initially distributed according to its quasistationary distribution. In particular, we work on domains in which the absorbing (Dirichlet) and reflecting (Neumann) parts of the boundary meet tangentially, without forming any non-trivial angle, a configuration that raises genuine regularity difficulties for the solutions of the associated mixed boundary value problem.

papers.title: Dual Quaternion Discrete Linear Canonical Transforms: Theory, Fast Algorithms, and Chirp-Adaptive Filtering for Rigid-Body Pose Signals
papers.abstract: We develop one- and two-dimensional dual quaternion discrete linear canonical transforms (DQ-DLCTs) for rigid-body pose signals, with left-, right-, and two-sided formulations that account for noncommutative kernel ordering. We establish inverse relations, kernel unitarity, energy preservation, perturbation stability, and spatial and frequency convolution relations. A chirp--Fourier--chirp factorization enables fast forward and inverse algorithms using complex FFTs, with two-dimensional complexity $\mathcal O(N_1N_2(\log N_1+\log N_2))$. For pose denoising, we introduce a two-stage chirp-adaptive method that estimates rotation before refining translation while enforcing unit-dual-quaternion constraints. Numerical experiments demonstrate agreement with direct transforms, substantial computational gains, and lower pose errors than the tested baselines on measured sequences and constructed two-dimensional fields. A downstream $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ synchronization study further demonstrates the potential of the proposed preprocessing approach, with performance depending on graph configurations. These results support efficient and geometry-aware processing of rigid-body pose signals.

papers.title: Millicharged particles and the degree-3 Prouhet-Tarry-Escott problem
papers.abstract: We use geometry to solve a problem in arithmetic relevant for physics. Namely, for any $m$ we find all integer solutions to the equations $\sum_{i=1}^m x_i^k = \sum_{i=1}^m y_i^k$, where $k \in \{1,2,3\}$; this seems to be new for $m \geq 5$. In physics, these are the anomaly cancellation conditions for models with $m$ fermions which can be naturally light and carry small electric charges (a.k.a. millicharged or minicharged particles). The small charges arise by kinetic mixing of the Standard Model $U(1)$ gauge symmetry with an unbroken non-chiral (a.k.a. vector-like) $U(1)$ and the masses are suppressed by a spontaneously-broken chiral $U(1)$.

papers.title: The second closed geodesic on Finsler manifolds with $\mathbb{Z}_2$ fundamental group
papers.abstract: Let $(M, F)$ be a compact bumpy Finsler manifold with $π_1(M)=\mathbb{Z}_2$, we prove that there exist at least two distinct non-contractible closed geodesics on $(M, F)$.

papers.title: Triple Overlap in Pipelined Krylov Methods on Multi-GPU Systems
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel triple-overlap implementation of the pipelined preconditioned conjugate gradient (Pipe-PCG) and pipelined stabilized biconjugate gradient (Pipe-BiCGStab) solvers, methods widely used in scientific applications. By leveraging a collective communication library, our approach extends conventional computation-communication overlap to concurrently execute collective operations, irregular P2P communication, and compute kernels, enabling computation-communication-communication overlap across multiple GPUs. We evaluate the design on the MareNostrum 5 (H100) and Leonardo (A100) supercomputers, comparing against PETSc and the state-of-the-art two-stream NCCL implementation using SuiteSparse matrices and three massive instances scaled up to 512 GPUs. The three-stream design outperforms the two-stream baseline on every instance, with the margin widening from 2-6% at 4 GPUs to 18-47% at 64 GPUs. At 64 GPUs, the geometric-mean speedup over the two-stream baseline is 1.33x on MareNostrum 5 and 1.23x on Leonardo for Pipe-PCG, and reaches 1.30x for Pipe-BiCGStab. In large-scale experiments, we observed a speedup up to 35% in Pipe-PCG and up to 33% in Pipe-BiCGStab compared to the two-stream design. For PETSc, the margin is even wider, up to 3.27x speedup in both Pipe-PCG and Pipe-BiCGStab. Related code for the proposed method is available online: https://github.com/ParCoreLab/aCG

papers.title: HEL: A Heterogeneous Extensible Layer for GPU-Resident Runtime Orchestration
papers.abstract: We describe a GPU-resident runtime system, HEL, built on stateful services that persist throughout the lifespan of a user application. A HEL programmer expresses a workload as an application that spawns coroutine-like tasks, which are then scheduled and run by the HEL runtime. HEL supports synchronous and asynchronous tasks, tasks with runtime dependencies, batched task submission, and automatic retries. Applications and tasks run alongside each other on the spatially partitioned GPU. Using producer-consumer and host-RPC benchmarks together with a PFPL compression case study, we show that HEL demonstrates a performance advantage for underutilized GPUs and for scenarios where HEL enables hiding task latency.

papers.title: Forecasting Patient Trajectories from the Electronic Health Records with Action-Conditioned World Models
papers.abstract: We introduce a predictive world model for electronic health records (EHR) that represents patient histories as action conditioned latent trajectories. Rather than modeling clinical events solely through autoregressive token prediction, our framework explicitly separates patient states from observed clinical actions and learns their evolution through a state and action conditioned transition operator. At its core is a state dependent linearization predictor that propagates local changes in latent patient state, enabling time resolved prediction, multi step rollout, and action conditioned simulation. Empirically, we show that generated latent trajectories preserve downstream predictive signal, temporal structure, and subgroup level statistical relationships present in encoder derived representations. We further decode free running rollouts into the original clinical feature space and evaluate future clinical measurements against observed values using task matched forecasting baselines, demonstrating that the learned dynamics retain predictive information beyond latent space agreement. Across binary classification and time to event tasks, EHR WM achieves competitive, though task dependent, performance relative to substantially larger EHR foundation models while using a 30x smaller parameter footprint. Finally, perturbing observed action sequences produces corresponding changes in generated trajectories, demonstrating the action sensitivity of the learned dynamics. Together, these results support world modeling as a complementary framework for learning explicit, time indexed representations of patient evolution from longitudinal EHR.

papers.title: Seven ordered points and the nonexistence of arithmetic ball quotient compactifications
papers.abstract: We prove that the ordered GIT quotient of seven points on $\mathbb P^1$ with equal weights is not isomorphic to the Baily--Borel compactification of any arithmetic complex ball quotient. Together with our companion paper and the known positive examples, this determines the equal weight case for every $n\ge6$: such a realization exists precisely for $n=6,8$. The lattice and the algebraic isomorphism are unrestricted, and torsion and divisorial ramification are allowed. The proof combines arithmetic reductions with identities involving Chern classes of fixed subvarieties and intersection inequalities for nef divisors on the GIT quotient. The final comparison includes all fixed components and requires no bound on the degree of an individual fixed curve.

papers.title: Provable Compliance: A Protocol for Runtime Compliance Evidence and Transaction-Specific Decisioning
papers.abstract: Regulated institutions already perform onboarding, screening, monitoring, and review, but compliance evidence ages, and whether it supports a decision depends on the institution, product, subject, counterparty, transaction, jurisdiction, risk tier, and purpose. A relying party therefore often cannot obtain compact, attributable proof of which evidence, policy, authority, and transaction context were current when a decision was made, a gap that grows as authority is delegated to software agents and scheduled workflows. We describe ChainIT Provable Compliance, the compliance-side layer of the ChainIT Authority Protocol. Each sourced or institution-generated fact is represented as a separate Evidence Assertion VDT with provenance, freshness, confidence, permitted purpose, and privacy classification; a versioned Compliance Policy Profile selects the applicable rules; a Business Rules Engine returns deterministic, reason-coded predicate results; and the organization's configured Workflow Engine composes them into a signed, time-bounded Compliance Decision VDT for one reliance event. The decision contributes a single predicate, Compliance Decision Permits, to session-eligibility and transaction-policy decisions. It never independently authorizes payment: only a final Allow together with an exact transaction digest, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use execution credential can commit value. The paper specifies point-of-reliance freshness, scoped propagation of evidence changes, decision states, evidence domains (AML, sanctions, PEP, background, identity, and licensing), the U.S. and FATF regulatory context as of August 2026, privacy and disclosure controls, and residual risks.

papers.title: Provable Authority: A Protocol for Verifiable Authority Resolution and Control Across Human, Organizational, and Agentic Transactions
papers.abstract: Payment systems authenticate users, devices, accounts, and cryptographic credentials, but a relying party, such as a counterparty, payment rail, marketplace, or autonomous agent runtime, generally cannot obtain compact, independently verifiable evidence that the party presenting one exact transaction holds current organizational authority to execute it under the applicable evidence, policy, budget, and approval state. Agentic commerce makes this gap operationally urgent: a software agent can produce a valid signature while acting outside its delegated purpose, after its sponsor's authority has changed, or on transaction details that differ from those a human approved. We describe the ChainIT Authority Protocol, a subject-neutral and rail-neutral pre-execution authority and evidence control plane. The protocol separates durable identity, a versioned organizational authority record (the Authority Resolution Pactvera), sourced evidence assertions, deterministic reason-coded policy predicates, and organization-configured dispositions; binds each decision and human approval to a canonical transaction digest; reserves capacity atomically so that limits hold under concurrency; and authorizes commit only through a single-use, sender-constrained Execution Authorization Credential consumed at the rail adapter, with append-only lifecycle evidence sealed after the terminal outcome. An Agent Subject Profile adds the workload registration, attested key hierarchy, and sovereignty boundary required when the acting subject is an AI agent, without introducing a separate authority concept. We specify the commit-time execution predicate and bounded-freshness status rules, give enforcement profiles for fiat (ACH, wire, card, instant payment) and stablecoin rails, and state residual risks and non-goals.

papers.title: On the two critical exponents for a dispersive equation with weak dissipation
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study a nonlinear Cauchy problem written in normal form \begin{equation*} \begin{cases} u_{tt} + A u+ Bu_t =D|u|^α, & t\geq 0, x \in \mathbb{R}^n\\ u(0,x)=u_0(x),\,u_t(0,x)=u_1(x). \end{cases} \end{equation*} Here~ $Af=\mathscr{F}^{-1}(a(ξ)^2\mathscr{F}f)$, with $a(ξ)$ homogeneous of order $k > 0$ under the assumption that the Hessian matrix of $a(ξ)$ is nonsingular, the operator $Bf=\mathscr{F}^{-1}(b(ξ)\mathscr{F}f)$ represents a weak dissipation, in the sense that $b(ξ) \sim 1$ as $|ξ| \to \infty$ and %, in several models, $D=B$ but we also consider the case $Df=ν\ast (-Δ)^δ(I-Δ)^{-δ}$, with $ν$ a bounded measure and $δ\geq k/2$. We derive $L^p-L^q$ estimates of the linear solution operator to the considered model and we prove the transition from a Fujita-type exponent to a Strauss-type exponent for the global-in-time existence of small data solution for the corresponding nonlinear problems.

papers.title: An infinite completely normal basis theorem
papers.abstract: Let $L/K$ be an arbitrary Galois extension with group $G$, equipped with the Krull topology. Let $C(G,K)$ denote the $K$-vector space of continuous functions $G\to K$, with $K$ discrete and $G$ acting by left translation. We prove that there exists a $G$-equivariant $K$-linear isomorphism $φ:C(G,K)\to L$ such that, for every open subgroup $H$ of $G$, the map $φ^H:C(H,L^H)\to L$ induced by extension by zero and extension of scalars is an $H$-equivariant $L^H$-linear isomorphism. This gives a completely normal analogue of Lenstra's infinite normal basis theorem.

papers.title: Locally Robust Inference with Outcomes Predicted by Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Many parameters of interest in economics depend on outcomes generated by machine learning (ML). These generated outcomes are subsequently used in standard econometric estimation and typically treated as observed, a practice that threatens the validity of downstream inference. Relevant examples include the partially linear model with an ML-predicted outcome, productivity persistence, and inequality of opportunity with life-cycle-corrected income. This paper develops a three-step locally robust GMM framework for valid inference when the dependent variable is generated by ML. We construct a debiased moment condition that augments the identifying moment with first- and second-step influence functions, making inference locally insensitive to regularization and model selection biases at both steps. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the locally robust estimator and illustrate its finite-sample performance through simulations. We then estimate inequality of opportunity in Spain, where incomes observed at different ages are subject to life-cycle bias. Correcting income for this bias with type-specific age profiles estimated by ML lowers inequality of opportunity over the working life by 10% to 14% relative to raw income, whereas treating the corrected incomes as observed overstates it by up to 15%.

papers.title: Hydrostatic Equilibrium Estimate of the Fuzzy Dark Matter Mass from Dwarf Spheroidals: Method and Systematics
papers.abstract: We present an estimator of an effective fuzzy (wave) dark matter (FDM) boson mass based on local hydrostatic equilibrium, which requires no soliton or other parametric density template. The condition requires the classical gravitational acceleration to be balanced by the gradient of the quantum potential in the Schrödinger--Poisson--Madelung system. We apply it to the density and enclosed-mass posteriors of nine Milky Way dwarf spheroidal (dSph) galaxies obtained with \textsc{pyGravSphere}. For each posterior realization, we determine by least squares the boson mass that best satisfies the force-balance condition over a fixed radial window. This gives a distribution of \(m_{21}\equiv m/10^{-21}\,\mathrm{eV}\) for each galaxy. The per-galaxy median masses range from \(m_{21}\sim 8\) to \(46\), corresponding to \(m\sim(0.8\text{--}4.6)\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{eV}\); Draco and Ursa Minor have the lowest median masses, while Carina and Sextans have the highest. The inverse-variance-weighted effective equilibrium mass of the nine galaxies is \(m=(1.31\pm0.35)\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{eV}\), with Draco and Ursa Minor contributing most of the weight. We also examine the systematic uncertainties in our results.

papers.title: Evo-DexBench: Benchmarking Generalization across Related Tasks for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.abstract: General-purpose dexterous manipulation requires policies to transfer knowledge from related tasks to new tasks with only a few target demonstrations. Existing benchmarks often provide too many target demonstrations and leave the differences between source and target tasks uncontrolled. As a result, they cannot clearly distinguish knowledge transfer from task memorization. Our key insight is the Core-Gen principle. Core tasks are related tasks that share a functional interaction and provide source knowledge, while a Gen task is a novel target within the same functional family that has only a few demonstrations. This setup tests whether a policy can reuse functional interaction knowledge. Based on this principle, we propose Evo-DexBench, which controls both source-task relatedness and target-task exposure. It comprises 30 tasks in six functional families, three everyday layouts per task, and 1,248 multimodal demonstrations collected via VR teleoperation with simulated Shadow Hands equipped with 123 taxels. We first compare few-shot adaptation strategies and find that joint Core + Gen training makes the most effective use of Core knowledge. Under this setting, we evaluate six representative policies. The best-performing policy, $π_{0.5}$, achieves a mean success rate of only 24.4%, revealing the limitations of existing methods in transferring functional interaction knowledge. Further analysis shows that on the tested Gen targets, functionally matched Core data yields larger success-rate gains than mismatched data, and that with matched Core data, 8 Gen demonstrations reach the performance of training on 16--32 Gen demonstrations alone. These results indicate that Evo-DexBench separates knowledge transfer from task memorization under controlled conditions and effectively evaluates the generalization of dexterous manipulation policies across related tasks.

papers.title: Conditional limit theorems for open intermittent dynamical systems
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study conditional limit theorems for open intermittent systems endowed with big/small holes. The initial measure for the system can be a class of (non)invariant probability, including the Lebesgue measure. Unlike the limit theorems for closed systems, we obtain an unexpected new limit distribution, which is not a stable law, for both "regular" and singular observables.

papers.title: SnapJudge: Multimodal AI Detection for Math-Heavy Scientific Text
papers.abstract: As large language models become increasingly capable of generating, and assisting with, scientific writing, there is a need for greater transparency and disclosure around the use of AI in research. Consequently, a veritable subfield of research and a number of commercial services aim to flag AI-generated content automatically. However, existing detectors which rely only on text extracted from PDFs fail to benefit from the rich visual information contained in the formatting of math-heavy scientific content. To study this, we select human-written proof and prose passages from pre-2022 arXiv LaTeX sources and re-generate them using 15 modern LLMs within the context of the same paper. This leaves us with coupled human and AI outputs in three different representations: the LaTeX source, a rendered image of the PDF, and the text extracted from the PDF. We find that the accuracy of the state-of-the-art Pangram 4 drops significantly as the mathematical content in a passage increases, especially when evaluated on text as opposed to LaTeX. However, this is not an inherent limitation of detecting AI-generated math: finetuning Qwen-3.5-27B based detectors on this domain recovers the gap, with LaTeX inputs performing significantly better than text since they preserve more formatting information. Since LaTeX sources are rarely available in practice, we also train SnapJudge: an image-based detector operating on screenshots of both prose and proofs from papers. At 0.1% false positive rate, SnapJudge achieves a detection rate of 92% on proofs and 93% on prose generated by frontier models, substantially outperforming both Pangram 4 and our text-based detector. We release our data, models and code at https://nlplab.cs.duke.edu/snapjudge.

papers.title: PRISM: Transfer and Limits of Activation Interventions in Tool-Calling Language Models
papers.abstract: Recent literature shows that unsafe tool calls can often accompany textual refusals in language models. To investigate this hidden vulnerability, we introduce PRISM, a framework for evaluating the transfer of activation interventions across precision, languages, and scales. Our findings demonstrate that leveraging lower-resource settings (specifically quantized NF4 labels and cross-lingual transfer) offers a robust pathway to expose and improve model alignment. Notably, using behavioral labels from an NF4 copy enables stable intervention estimation even with very few scenarios. Furthermore, these alignment improvements transfer effectively across languages: five-language NF4-supervised directions successfully transfer to held-out Arabic, reducing unsafe violations in Llama-3.1-8B by 21.95 percentage points without target-language tuning. By mapping paired benign activations, we also successfully transfer these safety interventions to much larger models (up to 70B parameters). Ultimately, PRISM highlights how auxiliary supervision from compressed models and multilingual data can uncover and mitigate hazardous tool-calling behaviors across different model families. We release all experimental code and supporting artifacts at https://github.com/GiKerche/prism, alongside an interactive explorer of recorded model responses and experimental results at https://gikerche.github.io/prism/.

papers.title: On the Hardy--Littlewood--Chowla conjecture
papers.abstract: An old conjecture dating back at least to Hildebrand's work in 1989, asserts that the Möbius function exhibits cancellation on shifted primes; that is, $$\sum_{p\le x}μ(p+2)=o(π(x)),\quad \text{or equivalently}\quad \sum_{n\le x}Λ(n)μ(n+2)=o(x).$$ This is also a well-known model case for the parity problem in sieve theory. In this paper, we prove this conjecture. As an application, we show that each of the two sets $\{p:\, μ(p+2)=1\}$ and $\{p:\, μ(p+2)=-1\}$ has asymptotic density $1/2$ among the primes $p$ with $μ^2(p+2)=1$: \begin{equation*} \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{\#\{p\le x:\ μ(p+2)=κ\}} {\#\{p\le x:\ μ^2(p+2)=1\}} =\frac12, \quad κ\in\{-1,\,1\}. \end{equation*}

papers.title: RPCA: a Resolved PSF reconstruction method for undersampled images
papers.abstract: The Point-Spread Function (PSF) is a critical component in various astrophysical research areas, including galaxy morphology, photometric redshift determination, and weak lensing studies. As the next generation of space telescopes prepares for operations, including the China Space Station Telescope (CSST), accurate PSF modeling has become increasingly important. However, accurately modeling the PSF remains challenging, particularly for poorly sampled images. To construct reliable PSF models based on star images, we aim to develop a novel and robust method, which accounts for the pixel integration effect in modeling for reconstructing high-resolution PSFs from undersampled or poorly resolved images. In this paper, we present Resolved Principal Components Analysis (RPCA), a novel approach that accounts for pixel integration effects to enable the direct reconstruction of resolved PSFs from undersampled images via an Expectation-Maximization PCA (EMPCA) technique. Our method has been tested on a simulated PSF dataset for the China Space Station Telescope (CSST), where both observational and detector-induced effects were considered during simulation. The results demonstrate that RPCA achieves superior precision in PSF shape parameters compared to existing methods such as Multi-CCD (MCCD), Resolved Components Analysis (RCA), and PSFEx. Notably, RPCA {could reduce the bias of $ΔR^2/R^2$ by approximately one order of magnitude with respect to MCCD, RCA and PSFEx. RPCA exhibits robust stability under realistic observational conditions, including varying signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) and contamination from cosmic rays and bad pixels. This suggests that RPCA could be a promising candidate for future CSST PSF modeling efforts.

papers.title: Magnetic field induced modulation of heat transport in CrPS$_4$ probed by TaIrTe$_4$ transverse Seebeck thermometry
papers.abstract: Understanding and controlling heat flow in low-dimensional magnetic materials is central to thermoelectrics and spin caloritronics. One of the challenges is the absence of sensitive probes of small, field-dependent modulations in thermal transport. Here we demonstrate transverse Seebeck thermometry using exfoliated TaIrTe$_4$ as a probe of thermal conductivity modulated by an external magnetic field on a van der Waals magnet, CrPS$_4$. With a temperature gradient oriented at $45^\circ$ to its principal crystallographic axes, TaIrTe$_4$ exhibits a transverse thermopower exceeding $200~\mathrm{μV\,K^{-1}}$ for 900 nm wide and 30 $μ$m long electrodes, enabling precise detection of variations in the local temperature gradients. Exploiting this with CrPS$_4$ in a nonlocal geometry, we resolve distinct field dependent thermal conductivity changes associated with both the spin-flip and spin-flop magnetic transitions which we attribute to variations in the magnon$-$phonon coupling in CrPS$_4$. At 5 K, the transverse Seebeck response is modulated by more than 8$\%$ by an external magnetic field, demonstrating strong magnetic control of heat transport in CrPS$_4$. This all van der Waals platform offers high sensitivity to modulations of thermal conductivity and a broad adaptability to a wide range of exfoliated magnetic systems.

papers.title: Refined Topology-Pass Scheduling: Damped Trust-Region Compensation for Dynamic k-NN Graphs in SE(3)-Equivariant Structure Prediction
papers.abstract: Equivariant structure-prediction pipelines alternate coordinate updates with the construction of a k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) graph whose membership is a discrete, piecewise-constant function of the coordinates. Rebuilding that graph at every block boundary (PB) is the expensive part of an epoch, whereas reusing one frozen graph (F) is fast but leaves a topology gap. We study a two-pass design in which the cheap pass records a small amount of state (margins, kNN radii, measured per-boundary displacements) and a second pass compensates conservatively. We formulate the choice of the graph-construction basis as a damped fixed-point iteration whose unique fixed point is exactly PB, and derive (i) exact non-flip certificates with the two-sided constant $m_i/4$ and one-sided constant $m_i/2$, (ii) the minimum-variance (BLUE) replay gain $γ^*$ and the resulting feasibility crossover, (iii) an $\ell_\infty$ trust-region projection that preserves convergence, and (iv) an analytic near-tie spacing law $E[m] \approx r_k/(3k)$ that matches measurements to 1\%. Three compensation levels are implemented in C++ (L1: frozen set with live geometry; L2: margin-gated local repair; L3: damped, projected basis) and validated under a matched-conditions protocol (identical seed, MSA depth and trajectory family, only the topology mode differs). L2 reproduces the PB edge set exactly ($D = 0.0000$ at every boundary), L1 stays within 0.6% and L3 interpolates monotonically: L2 reproduces the PB edge set exactly when the trust region is removed, and L3 interpolates between the frozen and the PB topology. The recorded trajectory itself yields a measured $1.5\times$ Pass-1 and $1.76\times$ epoch speed-up with no measurable loss gap. An open-source implementation of the runtime and of all the experiments reported here is available at https://github.com/AlbertHuang96/ProteinPredictMachineLearning.

papers.title: Non-Abelian quantum Hall states at strong Landau level mixing: finding anyons with first-principles AI
papers.abstract: Non-Abelian anyons, strange particles forming the basis of fault-tolerant topological quantum computing, are predicted to emerge in fractional quantum Hall states at even-denominator filling factors. Identifying which topological order is realized has proven to be a challenging problem that requires an accurate, non-perturbative treatment of realistic Landau level mixing, which has so far been missing from theoretical studies. Here we present the first complete solution of non-Abelian quantum Hall problem that includes all electrons and all Landau levels, for spin-polarized electrons at filling factor $ν= 3/2$. We develop a momentum-resolved neural-network variational wave function, optimized solely on the microscopic Hamiltonian, which gives direct access to the topologically degenerate ground states. Without any physics input about the expected outcome, it discovers a degenerate ground-state manifold whose entanglement reveals anyons with quantum dimension $\sqrt{2}$, the hallmark of Ising-type non-Abelian order. By directly computing the overlap with trial wave functions, we further show that Landau level mixing favors the anti-Pfaffian over other candidate states. Our results demonstrate the power of neural-network wave functions in finding and characterizing non-Abelian anyons from first principles, in regimes of strong Landau level mixing, relevant to many recent experiments.

papers.title: Solomonoff induction of selected bits and online classification
papers.abstract: Solomonoff induction is a general solution for sequence prediction that started the field of algorithmic information theory around 1960. Let $M$ be the universal semimeasure. After observing a string $ω_1 \cdots ω_{n-1}$, it predicts the next bit $ω_n$ to be $b$ with conditional probability proportional to $M(ω_1 \cdots ω_{n-1} b)$. Thus the error of this probability is \[ e_ω(n) = 1 - \frac {M(ω_1 \cdots ω_{n-1}ω_n)} {M(ω_1 \cdots ω_{n-1} 0) + M(ω_{1} \cdots ω_{n-1} 1)}. \] If $ω$ a computable infinite sequence with a self-delimiting description of at most $k$ bits, then $\sum_n e_ω(n) \le k\ln 2+O(1)$. Lattimore, Hutter and Gavane consider the problem of predicting computable patterns in a sequence, for example, the pattern of repeated bits $ω= 00\,11\,00\,00\,11\,00\cdots$ They show that the error probabilities of the bits fixed by a computable pattern have limit zero, for example, for repeated bits, one has $\lim_n e_ω(2n) = 0$. We show that for some computable pattern, the sum of $e_ω(n)$ over positions $n$ from the pattern is not bounded. However, the sum of squares $(e_ω(n))^2$ is bounded exponentially in the program length of the pattern. It is also shown that bits of $ω$ that are fixed by a computable classification function $f:\{0,1\}^* \rightarrow \{0,1\}$, converges faster: the sum of $(e_ω(n))^2$ is bounded by a polynomial in the program length for programs whose runtime is bounded by any fixed computable time bound.

papers.title: ResearchFlow-Eval: Tracing the Execution Gap in End-to-End Multi-Claim Autoresearch
papers.abstract: Autoresearch systems increasingly undertake entire research projects. In practice, scientific research requires systems to pursue multiple interdependent claims through a continuous, multi-stage workflow and revise experiments as evidence accumulates. Existing evaluations of autoresearch systems, however, typically score isolated tasks or final artifacts, leaving these process-level capabilities largely unmeasured. We therefore introduce ResearchFlow-Eval, a fine-grained framework for assessing continuous scientific execution and iteration at both the stage and claim levels. Each evaluation is grounded in a published anchor paper, from which we derive stage-specific rubrics that decompose each research stage into dimensions and separately scored rubric items. Using these rubrics, we score each research stage and examine experimental execution in detail, focusing on multi-claim completion and revisions across attempts. We apply the evaluation framework to general-purpose agent harnesses, skill-augmented harnesses, and systems with research-specific orchestration. Averaged over two runs per system, each scored by two LLM judges, experimental execution lags behind design and planning for every evaluated system. Within execution, systems struggle to produce high-quality results and meet claim requirements, and repeated attempts rarely yield measurable improvements. Moreover, neither skill augmentation nor research-specific orchestration reliably yields higher scores. ResearchFlow-Eval thus extends autoresearch evaluation beyond isolated, single-objective runs to continuous workflows in which systems pursue multiple claims and refine their work across iterations.

papers.title: Releasing the Inner Jev: A Simple Recipe for Open Decision Models
papers.abstract: LLM-based decision-making systems, also called System One models, have recently gained popularity, most notably through Jev (Almeida, 2026). Given a typed input state, a question, and a set of options, they return a calibrated probability for each option in a single forward pass, without text generation. We show that open instruction-tuned LLMs can achieve performance comparable to Jev without any additional training, by reading out answers from letters (A, B, C, etc.) in the model's output logits at the last token position. Next, we propose a simple supervised LoRA fine-tuning recipe that can improve their performance further. We evaluate four instruction-tuned LLMs: Gemma 4 31B, Gemma 4 12B, Qwen3.6-27B, and Qwen3.5-4B. Furthermore, we introduce OpenDecisions, a novel 2,352-question validation dataset designed to reflect the task composition of JevBench (JevBench maintainers, 2026) and which computes a Capability score based on accuracy and calibration. Without fine-tuning, Gemma 4 31B scores 79.6 on OpenDecisions, compared to Jev's 80.1. After fine-tuning, it scores 89.0, outperforming Jev by 8.9 Capability points and on par with the strongest open decision model we evaluated. The same recipe improves the three other models by 7.8 to 15.7 points. On a suite of public decision datasets, our models achieve accuracy and calibration comparable to Jev. Our results show that open LLMs already possess System One capabilities, and with simple fine-tuning they outperform Jev on a wide range of decision tasks. We release our models, training and serving code, OpenDecisions, and DecisionBank, our training dataset consisting of 261,561 decisions.

papers.title: A Cauchy Busemann function approach to the geometry of cosmological spacetimes with applications to Bartnik's conjecture
papers.abstract: We study the geometry of future timelike complete spacetimes admitting a compact Cauchy hypersurface. Future timelike completeness is compatible with an initial singularity and disregards the incompleteness expected inside black holes, so it is a reasonable large scale idealization for a Universe without final singularity. Given a compact Cauchy hypersurface $Σ$, we introduce the future Cauchy Busemann function $b^+$. Its finiteness domain, the future cosmological development, and its boundary, the future cosmological horizon, do not depend on $Σ$. For spacetimes with an initial singularity, namely with regular cosmological time, we obtain a canonical Cauchy Busemann function and a canonical calibrating semi-flow. Using a product trick we show that $b^+$ is the graph function of a Cauchy horizon in $M\times \mathbb{R}$: $b^+$ is locally Lipschitz and locally semi-concave on the future development, the future horizon is a $C^0$ null hypersurface, and through every point of the development passes a calibrated timelike ray, an observer who ages maximally into the far future. We give a foliation-free formula for $b^+$ as a minimal asymptotic clock defect. Under the timelike convergence condition (TCC) the level sets of $b^+$ are mean convex in the support sense. We apply these results to Bartnik's splitting conjecture for timelike complete spacetimes satisfying the TCC. If the future and past cosmological developments intersect, which happens whenever $b^+$ is $C^1$ on its finiteness domain, then the spacetime contains a timelike line and hence splits. Therefore any counterexample contains a non-empty closed causally convex set, the cosmological wall, separating the two developments; some component of the future horizon contains a lightlike line, and if the wall has empty interior it coincides with both horizons and is ruled by lightlike lines.

papers.title: Cone Restriction Estimates under Half-Scale Dimensional Conditions
papers.abstract: We prove cone restriction estimates under half-scale dimensional conditions. Building on the framework of Du--Li--Wang--Zhang, we incorporate the broad restriction estimate of Ou--Wang and a localized multilinear estimate obtained through cyclic bilinear pairing and multilinear Kakeya bounds for local packet $L^2$-norm. The zero-dimensional case yields a large-value estimate on $R^{1/2}$-cubes. For certain ambient and weight dimensions, our estimates are sharp in suitable ranges of $p$, up to an $R^\varepsilon$ loss.

papers.title: Neural Estimation of Irreversibility in Real and Simulated Limit Order Book Paths
papers.abstract: A path indistinguishable from its own reverse carries no arrow of time, so time irreversibility is a necessary condition for a directed mechanism to be readable from trajectories alone. In finance it has been measured only on scalar series such as returns and volatility. We define the irreversibility rate of a coarse-grained limit order book path as the forward-to-reverse log-density ratio per event, and estimate it from three weeks of Nasdaq market-by-order data with an order-invariant MLP and a temporal convolutional network that receive identical blocks. For NVDA, the order-invariant and order-sensitive estimates are 0.036 and 0.054 nats per event, respectively. Their difference, the ordering increment, is 0.018. A surrogate preserving the coarse one-step transition table recovers 30 percent less irreversibility than the observed paths. The increment is positive for all twelve symbols on every held-out daytime date, and for NVDA in each session window. Across the twelve symbols, its share of the ordered rate increases roughly logarithmically with the spread in ticks. The increment changes more than tenfold with the coarse-graining scale. Neither a linear score nor any single feature group reproduces the full fitted rate. A queue-reactive simulator calibrated on the same days matches the market's ordered rate, 0.052 against 0.054, yet its ordering increment is 0.0006 against 0.018, building temporal asymmetry out of block composition instead of block order. We propose the ordering and scale profile of path irreversibility as a benchmark for order book simulators. Code and audit materials are available at https://github.com/hjyeo30/lob-irreversibility.

papers.title: HDKEM: Authentication Allocation for Deniable Hybrid Key Exchange
papers.abstract: A deniable authenticated key exchange (DAKE) establishes an authenticated shared key without giving third parties proof of participation. Post-quantum DAKEs use ring signatures, message authentication codes, or split key-encapsulation mechanisms, which differ in who can authenticate and how deniability is achieved. We introduce \emph{authentication allocation} to classify which parties hold secrets that produce accepted authentication messages. For protocols using a fixed two-member ring, we prove that an accuser can simulate a session by either sharing the accused party's authentication key or signing with its own ring key. Thus, deniability relies on key sharing or the ring signature's ability to hide its signer. We propose \HDKEM, combining ML-KEM-768, X25519, and an optional pre-shared or quantum key distribution (QKD)-delivered key $k_3$ through a split-key pseudorandom function. The session key remains secret if at least one input remains secure. Since provisioning services and QKD key managers may know $k_3$, the client always authenticates with its own ring key; the mode determines whether other holders of $k_3$ can impersonate the server. Four modes are supported: \emph{source-backed} authenticates the server through key confirmation under $k_3$, allowing its holders to impersonate the server; \emph{hide} also encrypts the client's signature; \emph{mutual} adds a server ring signature to prevent such impersonation; and \emph{source-less} authenticates both endpoints with ring signatures without $k_3$. We prove extended Canetti--Krawczyk (eCK) session-key secrecy in the quantum random-oracle model, explicit authentication, forward secrecy, and session-partner deniability, with a concrete deniability bound in the classical random-oracle model. With FalconRS, source-backed mode sends 3,813~bytes in about 26~ms, versus 5,101~bytes and 47~ms in mutual mode.

papers.title: QuasiStim: Scalable Accurate Non-Pauli Noise Simulation for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computer design relies on simulating noisy quantum error correction (QEC) circuits with hundreds to thousands of physical qubits and large circuit depths. High-throughput stabilizer simulators, such as Stim, are the de facto tools for this regime. However, these simulators typically support only Clifford gates and stochastic Pauli noise. As a result, more realistic device noise models, such as coherent control errors and thermal relaxation, are often approximated using Pauli twirling. This replacement offers speed but can introduce substantial inaccuracies. To address this, we propose QuasiStim for scalable, accurate QEC simulation of realistic noise, with QuasiFold as a compiler frontend and DeltaFrame as a sampling backend. QuasiFold lowers sampling overhead by opportunistically merging non-Pauli noise sites in the quantum circuit without changing the circuit output. DeltaFrame samples the resulting stabilizer trajectories by reusing precomputed predicted references instead of resimulating the full tableau for each shot. In our evaluation, QuasiFold can reduce the number of shots by over $1000\times$ on bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes under coherent $R_{ZZ}$ noise. Compared to a per-shot tableau simulator, DeltaFrame is $190\times$ to $1479\times$ faster on rotated surface-code memory as $d$ grows from 5 to 35. QuasiStim also makes the PTA bias measurable: the gap is non-trivial and varies with noise strength, decoder, and circuit schedule.

papers.title: A new approach to interior estimates for fully nonlinear elliptic equations
papers.abstract: We give new proofs of interior second derivative estimates for the quadratic Hessian and Monge-Ampère equations with Dini continuous right-hand sides. Our approach uses a three-point maximum principle and requires no differentiation of the equations. For the quadratic Hessian equation, the estimate holds in every dimension $n\ge2$. For the Monge-Ampère equation, the proof is localised on sublevel sets of a strictly convex solution.

papers.title: Mixing Regularization for Average-Reward $Q$-Learning and $Q$-Planning
papers.abstract: The average-reward setting for reinforcement learning is challenging because, without discounting, the span-contraction of the Bellman operator depends on the mixing properties of the underlying Markov dynamics. Whereas existing work typically assumes contraction, for instance through environment mixing, we study regularization toward a given reward-agnostic, $m$-step mixing policy to control the mixing properties of the learned policy. Our central mixing lemma quantifies how the reference policy's mixing properties transfer to the resulting learned policies. In particular, a single regularizer-dependent quantity simultaneously controls the contraction of the regularized Bellman operator and the exploration of the resulting policies. A second regularizer-dependent quantity controls the bias introduced by regularization, revealing a trade-off between convergence speed and approximation accuracy. Building on this result, we establish finite-time guarantees for regularized $Q$-iteration, synchronous and single-trajectory $Q$-learning, and $Q$-planning. Under one-step mixing, our bounds for approximating the regularized fixed point match the classical model-query bound for relative value iteration and, up to logarithmic factors, an existing sample-complexity bound for synchronous $Q$-learning. We also establish finite-time guarantees under multi-step mixing. For $Q$-planning, we characterize how the planning horizon trades off boundary bias against sample complexity. Finally, we present numerical studies validating the analysis: (i) knowledge of a strong mixing policy improves convergence and exploration, with larger benefits under more severe bottlenecks; and (ii) the observed rankings of $α$-divergence regularizers by bias and convergence speed are consistent with our theoretical analysis.

papers.title: Composable Driving Style for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies can achieve strong task performance while offering limited control over their driving style. Driving style describes how a vehicle accelerates, brakes, and maintains distance. Policies trained without explicit preference conditioning lack a direct mechanism for adjusting these behaviors at inference. We propose YOUDrive, a vision--language--action planner for continuous and composable driving-style control. Each teacher's behavior is distilled into a task vector, a learned parameter update that induces a style direction in the planner's representation. These directions can be scaled and combined at inference without retraining the backbone. Conditioned on these directions, a flow-matching decoder models a multimodal trajectory distribution and generates kinematically feasible motion alternatives. We introduce the Style Alignment Score (SAS) to describe human-referenced kinematic behavior after safety and task gating. On NAVSIM navtest, a single coefficient monotonically controls assertiveness across six teacher-derived personas, while PDMS remains above 0.90 across the tested individual and blended configurations, reaching 0.954. Further analyses reveal systematic policy-specific kinematics after controlling for scene context, whereas the evaluated discrete style labels provide limited additional explanatory power. Code, checkpoints, and the metric will be released.

papers.title: A note on Guo's perturbation result for symmetric nonnegative matrices
papers.abstract: In 1997 Guo Wuwen proved that if $(λ_1,λ_2,\dots,λ_n)$ is the spectrum of a nonnegative matrix with Perron eigenvalue $λ_1$ and $λ_2$ real, then $(λ_1+t,λ_2\pm t,λ_3,\dots,λ_n)$ is the spectrum of a nonnegative matrix for every $t\ge 0$. Whether the same holds for symmetric nonnegative matrices has remained an open question. We give an affirmative answer, in a slightly stronger form: if $A$ is a symmetric nonnegative matrix with Perron eigenvalue $λ_1$ and further eigenvalues $λ_2,\dots,λ_n$, and $d_1\ge|d_2|+\dots+|d_n|$, then there is a symmetric matrix $B\ge A$ with eigenvalues $λ_1+d_1,\dots,λ_n+d_n$, and $B$ has the same diagonal as $A$ when $d_1+\dots+d_n=0$. This leads us to call a symmetrically realizable list \emph{Guo-extreme} if none of Guo's moves can be reversed for this list. Every symmetrically realizable list is a Guo-extreme list plus a vector from the cone of Guo's moves. Our second main result is a certificate, modeled on a theorem of Laffey on extreme symmetric matrices: if every nonnegative symmetric matrix that commutes with $A$ and is equal to zero on the entries where $A$ is positive is a multiple of the identity, then $A$ is orthogonally similar to a positive matrix if $A$ has a positive diagonal entry, and to a matrix with zero diagonal and positive off-diagonal entries if $A$ has zero diagonal. Consequently, the spectrum of $A$ can be moved by a small amount in every direction, respectively in every trace-preserving direction, and remain symmetrically realizable. In particular, the spectrum of such a matrix is not Guo-extreme.

papers.title: PILOT: Guiding Long-Horizon World-Model Planning for Robot Manipulation with Imagined Subgoals and Policy Priors
papers.abstract: Latent world-model planning has shown promising results in goal-conditioned robotic manipulation, but remains challenging for long-horizon planning due to limited temporal guidance and inefficient action search. A distant goal image offers little guidance for preparatory actions, capturing intermediate subgoal images by hand is impractical, and uninformed sampling makes action search inefficient. We propose PILOT (Policy-Initialized Local Optimization with Temporal subgoals), which brings two foundation models into latent world-model planning: a video model turns a language instruction into visual subgoals, and a vision-language-action policy initializes the cross-entropy method (CEM). CEM refines action sequences toward each subgoal with an action-conditioned world model, and no goal image is needed at test time. With both models fine-tuned on 40 demonstrations, PILOT achieves 68.8% success on four real UR5e tasks, compared with 55.0% without policy initialization, 13.8% for policy-only execution, and 0.0% for direct final-goal planning. In simulation, PILOT exceeds direct execution of the same policy by 30 percentage points on long Push-T tasks and by 22 percentage points on LIBERO-10. Subgoals and the policy prior are complementary: better subgoals and stronger priors each raise success, and even a weak policy that succeeds alone on only 3.3% of medium Push-T tasks is an effective prior.

papers.title: Revealing New Leakage Paths in GAAFETs using Predictive First-Principles Simulations
papers.abstract: Gate-All-Around Field-Effect Transistors (GAAFETs) are emerging as successors to Fin Field-Effect Transistors (FinFETs) and are central to continued scaling at advanced semiconductor nodes. Despite their improved electrostatic control, recent measurements show that the drain current in GAAFETs deviates strongly from thermionic behavior at negative gate voltages, increasing as the gate voltage becomes more negative. This leakage has been attributed to direct gate-drain tunneling through the high-$k$ dielectric, enhanced by drain-induced dielectric barrier lowering (DIDBL). Here, we use predictive, charge-self-consistent Non-Equilibrium Green Function (NEGF) simulations based on the Contact Block Reduction (CBR) method to spatially resolve this leakage pathway in GAAFETs. Unlike approaches based primarily on phenomenological leakage models, our first-principles, multi-terminal quantum-transport framework treats the source, drain, and gate as current-carrying quantum-mechanical contacts and resolves the local current density throughout the device. The spatially resolved current density shows that gate-injected carriers tunnel through the high-$k$ dielectric preferentially near the drain side of the gate, where the dielectric barrier is most strongly lowered by the drain bias, and are collected by the drain. This provides a direct real-space picture of the DIDBL-driven gate-drain leakage mechanism.

papers.title: Cluster Ages to Reconstruct the Milky Way Assembly (CARMA). VI. The age-metallicity relation of in-situ clusters and the age of the Universe
papers.abstract: Within the homogeneous framework for the derivation of GC ages defined by the CARMA collaboration, we focus on the clusters born in-situ in the MW. As they are the oldest among the old GCs, their absolute age provides constraints about the age of the Universe. Moreover, the shape of their AMR is expected to show the imprints of past merger events, in case these were able to trigger GC formation in the Galaxy. We derive new homogeneous ages for 18 GCs dynamically and/or chemically classified as in-situ, and build the MW AMR from a total sample of 34 GCs. We find that all the selected GCs follow a well defined AMR, with the exception of NGC6642 and Pal1. While the former is likely a member of the LKH merger event, thus putting chronological evidence for the existence of this progenitor on even more robust ground, for the latter we propose an alternative scenario according to which it formed in-situ, but in a metal-depleted region of the Galaxy, possibly due to the interaction with an unspecified merger event. To find evidence of merger-driven GC formation, we use a GMM for the observed age distribution. This is statistically best-fit by 4 components, which we associate with significant events of the MW merger history. Cluster ages were finally calibrated to a more accurate absolute age scale based on asteroseismic measurements of the mass of red giant stars in NGC6791, and the resulting AMR was fit to compute the look-back time for the beginning of cluster formation in the MW. The fit yields t_GC,i=13.59+0.33-0.32 Gyr for initial cluster formation, and tU=13.79+/-0.34 Gyr for the age of the Universe. This value translates to H0=68.72+3.95-3.49(stat.)+2.65-2.32(sys.) km s-1 Mpc-1, where the systematic error comes from a realistic estimate of the zero point uncertainty on the GC absolute ages derived from stellar models.

papers.title: Digraph Laplacian spectra: The 2005 polygon conjecture fails for all orders above four
papers.abstract: Let $Λ_n$ be the set of all eigenvalues of standardized Laplacian matrices of order $n$, equivalently, of stochastic $n\times n$ matrices with off-diagonal entries at most $\frac1n$. In 2005, a polygon $S_n\subseteqΛ_n$ was constructed, and it was conjectured that $Λ_n=S_n$; this holds for $n\le3$. We show that the conjecture fails for every $n\ge5$. The vertices of $S_n$ are eigenvalues of circulant Laplacians built from powers of the directed $n$-cycle. To first order, no perturbation of these circulants moves such an eigenvalue out of $S_n$; however, adding chords with nonconstant weights moves it along an edge of $S_n$ to first order and, with an explicit coefficient, beyond the supporting line of this edge to second order. Consequently, every edge of $S_n$ not incident to $0$ or $1$ contains interior points of $Λ_n$, except possibly, for even $n$, the two horizontal edges, whereas the four edges incident to $0$ or $1$ lie on $\partialΛ_n$. For $n=4$, whose only other edges are horizontal, the question has recently been settled, $Λ_4=S_4$, by computer-assisted proofs of D. Z. Liu and L. Marshall; Liu also proved that $Λ_n$ is not convex for $n\ge5$. We certify an explicit weighted counterexample for $n=5$, lying only $1.5\cdot10^{-3}$ outside $S_5$, and an unweighted one for $n=7$: the directed $6$-cycle with a duplicated vertex. Its eigenvalue outside $S_7$ is also an eigenvalue of the two-chord digraph that ends the above perturbation; for the analogous digraphs of order $n$, the excess is asymptotic to $\frac{π^2}{2n^4}$. We also observe that $S_n$ is a zonotope, describe $Λ_n$ in terms of eigenvectors, and prove that $S_m\subseteq S_n$ whenever $m\mid n$.

papers.title: $L_0$ Feature Selection via Monte Carlo Tree Search in High-Dimensional Financial Regression
papers.abstract: Feature selection is a central problem in high-dimensional financial regression, where large numbers of engineered variables and strong correlations among predictors reduce model stability and interpretability. $L_1$ regularization (Lasso) is widely used for sparse regression, but its shrinkage can be restrictive when informative signals are spread across correlated variables. Exact sparse regression avoids this shrinkage but requires solving a combinatorial optimization problem that is computationally difficult and is typically fit to minimize in-sample rather than out-of-sample error. This paper presents a feature selection framework based on Monte Carlo Tree Search with Generalized Nested Rollout Policy Adaptation (GNRPA). Feature selection is formulated as a sequential decision process, and candidate subsets are scored by their out-of-sample validation performance rather than training error. The method also supports a lexicographic objective accounting for subset size and multicollinearity. We study this approach on a contemporaneous explanatory regression task: explaining the weekly return of the NASDAQ-100 index from 1,072 engineered features spanning market, macroeconomic, and factor data. This isolates the value of subset selection under multicollinearity from the separate problem of predictive forecasting. On this task, the proposed method identifies sparse feature subsets with higher out-of-sample explanatory power than an optimized Lasso baseline, reaching an out-of-sample $R^2$ of 0.6961 versus 0.6313 for Lasso. These results suggest that Monte Carlo Tree Search is a practical alternative to convex regularization for sparse explanatory feature selection in financial regression, with potential value for factor attribution and risk decomposition where transparency matters as much as out-of-sample fit.

papers.title: SplatQ: Interaction-Aware Pruning of 3D Gaussian Splatting via Quadratic Selection
papers.abstract: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pruning methods primarily rely on global Top-K selection based on independent importance scores, lacking regional budget control and ignoring joint deletion effects. Consequently, they cannot ensure balanced reconstruction quality across a scene. We propose SplatQ, a combinatorial pruning algorithm that coordinates regional budget allocation and joint Gaussian selection under a fixed budget. SplatQ partitions Gaussians by spatial proximity and appearance similarity into size-limited blocks, decomposing global selection into subproblems of a specific size. It then smooths importance-based block retention quotas to prevent excessive budget concentration. Finally, it constructs a quadratic approximation of joint deletion effects using the responses of representative pixel colors to changes in Gaussian opacity. Individual responses, pairwise interactions, and quota penalties are incorporated into a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) objective, solved using simulated annealing (SA) or a coherent Ising machine (CIM) to jointly select Gaussians. Experiments on 5 benchmarks demonstrate that SplatQ outperforms state-of-the-art pruning methods in aggregate reconstruction quality, spatial quality balance, and rendering speed. Ablations confirm that budget smoothing improves local detail reconstruction, while interaction modeling improves Gaussian selection quality under a fixed budget.

papers.title: Localization Landscapes based on the Green's Matrix of Non-Hermitian Optical Scattering Systems
papers.abstract: The Filoche--Mayboroda (FM) localization landscape predicts where the spatially localized modes of a self-adjoint elliptic operator reside without diagonalizing it, but the construction fails for the complex, non-normal Green's matrix G of an open scattering array of electric dipoles. We propose three real-valued, positive landscapes built from the Feinberg--Zee hermitization of G: a regularized Gramian inverse (Gram), the diagonal Schur block that carries the Metz--Neri--Rogers spectral density (SY), and the full hermitized inverse contracted against a uniform source (TM) or an isotropic polarization pair (TE) (Herm). The three form a progression from spectrum-blind to fully hermitization-faithful, agree in the limit $z\to 0$, and diverge where it matters: at nonzero spectral shift SY resolves modes that Gram collapses, and Herm resolves modes that SY collapses. We demonstrate the progression on random and deterministic aperiodic scattering arrays with a wide range of structural correlations, extend to the vectorial case of transverse electric polarization (TE), and provide rigorous pointwise envelope bounds for the Spec and Herm landscapes, a physical argument for the spatial compactness of long-lived modes, and a complete numerical recipe in the appendices.

papers.title: Percolation of Data Constraints and Reorganization of Boolean Function States in Parity Learning
papers.abstract: We study how a neural network reorganizes its learned function as training proceeds and as previously unseen parity data accumulate. The trained model is itself a Boolean function on binary strings of finite length. We then evaluate it on all data, inside and outside the training set, and read off its complete sign table. Its $\pm1$ entries are the amplitudes of a normalized state, dubbed the function-state, whose inverse subsystem purity $K_f=1/\textrm{Tr}(ρ_A^2)$ is an effective Schmidt rank. We find that small data additions broaden the Schmidt spectrum, whereas larger additions reconcentrate it in the target mode. The former is called differentiation because the model distinguishes inputs more sharply. The latter is called target-selective recoherence, where the model settles on the single rule shared by the added data. As the dataset grows, the connectivity of the constraint graph defined by the training set increases monotonically, whereas the learned inverse purity changes nonmonotonically. On a fixed connected dataset, as learning proceeds, the Schmidt spectrum begins to reorganize, followed by gains in target alignment and later by improvement in predictive accuracy. This ordering distinguishes three aspects of learning: constraint identifiability, function-state organization, and predictive accuracy. At fixed data size, a function that has already been learned can re-differentiate, an event we call retreat, without changing graph connectivity. Recovery reconcentrates the Schmidt spectrum in a similar target-selective pattern, without exact recurrence of the Boolean state. Thus the percolation of data constraints fixes the identifiable support, while the reduced state produced by training continues to reorganize even after that support stops changing.

papers.title: Cross-Behavior Policy Optimization: Unified Learning from Offline Demonstrations and On- and Off-Policy Rollouts via a Shared Regression Target
papers.abstract: Reasoning post-training draws on offline demonstrations and policy-generated rollouts, yet conventional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL) separates their objectives and limits continued reuse of collected responses. We propose \textbf{Cross-Behavior Policy Optimization} (CBPO), which makes these sources compatible with one regression loss through a fixed-reference target. Because the generating policy does not enter this target, positive and negative offline completions, reference responses, and current and historical rollouts can share a common reward-labeled record format and replay buffer. As new responses enter the buffer, optimization retains the same regression objective without coordinating separate SFT and RL objectives or requiring stored behavior-policy probabilities, importance weighting, or a learned critic. Restricting the available sources gives offline, on-policy, and off-policy variants, while CBPO-Unified combines them. Across two model scales and four mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CBPO delivers leading \texttt{avg@32} and \texttt{pass@32} performance across benchmarks and data regimes. On Qwen3-1.7B, CBPO-Unified improves benchmark-averaged \texttt{avg@32} and \texttt{pass@32} over SFT DAPO by 2.33 and 4.44 percentage points, respectively. In the replay ablation, retaining historical rollouts improves these metrics by 1.87 and 3.72 percentage points over the no-history configuration.

papers.title: Mass and decay angles in the $Ξ_c$--$Ξ_c'$ mixing tension: Virtual hybrids and a single-direction criterion
papers.abstract: We compare three definitions of $Ξ_c$--$Ξ_c'$ mixing within a constituent-quark model: a spin-component probability angle, a common-source overlap angle, and an SU(3)-breaking mass-operator angle. The probability angle is $3.11^\circ$, while the two operator-based definitions give $2.48$--$2.58^\circ$; a second parameter set gives $2.38$--$2.49^\circ$. The operator-based angles are closer to the lattice determinations $1.2(1)^\circ$ and $0.810(50)(200)^\circ$, but remain larger. We then couple conventional $qsQ$ states to virtual $qsQg$ configurations, where $q=u,d$ and $Q=c,b$. An orbital-$S$-wave chromomagnetic transition containing both $j_{Qg}=1/2$ and $3/2$ raises the source and mass-operator charm angles to $2.67$--$3.16^\circ$ when normalized to reference short-range mass shifts. The hybrid probability stays below $1.7\%$, and the corresponding bottom angles are $0.42$--$0.48^\circ$. Eliminating the hybrid sector gives a rank-one mass correction precisely when all weighted transitions select the same retained-state combination. The mode-resolved calculation separates the flavor-breaking response that changes the mixing angle from the response that generates a second transition direction. The accompanying effective-current relation connects this mass analysis to radiative and semileptonic amplitudes through their current matrix elements.

papers.title: asdex: Automatic Sparse Differentiation in JAX
papers.abstract: Many tasks in scientific computing and machine learning require the Jacobian or Hessian matrix of a function. Automatic differentiation (AD) computes these derivatives to machine precision, but materializing a dense $m \times n$ Jacobian requires $n$ forward-mode or $m$ reverse-mode AD passes, one per column or row. For a large class of functions, each output depends on only a few inputs, making the derivative matrix sparse. Automatic sparse differentiation (ASD) exploits this structure in four steps: detection of the input-agnostic sparsity pattern, coloring of a graph to group columns or rows that can share an AD pass, compressed differentiation to compute a compressed derivative matrix with one AD pass per color, and finally decompression into the original sparsity pattern. The number of colors, and hence of AD passes, is often independent of the problem dimension: a banded Jacobian with $b$ contiguous bands, for instance, only ever requires $b$ colors, regardless of its size. asdex offers the first standalone ASD toolkit in the popular JAX ecosystem. With asdex$.$jacobian and asdex$.$hessian, it provides sparse drop-in replacements for jax$.$jacobian and jax$.$hessian.

papers.title: MultiWorldBench: Do Independently Controlled Views Describe One Shared World?
papers.abstract: Multiplayer world models must ensure that independently controlled views remain consistent with a single shared and persistent world. We introduce MultiWorldBench, a diagnostic Minecraft benchmark comprising 495 case configurations across seven task suites and ten capabilities, including independent control, cross-view motion, shared-state synchronization, persistence, structural reasoning, concurrent interaction, and delayed revisit. Using Engine GT as a reference, we evaluate two multiplayer world models, Solaris (MP) and Gamma-World, together with a single-player generation variant, Solaris (SP). Among the generated systems, Gamma-World achieves the highest ten-capability average at 21.39, followed by Solaris (MP) at 20.88 and Solaris (SP) at 10.06, while Engine GT reaches 91.69. Gamma-World performs better on several control, shared-state, and revisit capabilities, whereas Solaris (MP) leads in cross-view motion and race-condition consistency. Nevertheless, all generated systems score at most 8.00 on state persistence and 1.33 on structural consistency, and none succeeds in spatial reasoning or building-identity preservation. Human pairwise evaluation yields the same overall system ranking and shows strong alignment with the automatic evaluation, with a mean dimension-level Spearman correlation of 0.95. These results show that current multiplayer world models still exhibit a substantial gap relative to Engine GT in maintaining a coherent shared world.

papers.title: The Binary Fraction of Milky Way Field Stars in DESI: Dependence on Chemical Abundances
papers.abstract: Binary populations encode information about the physical conditions of star formation and the subsequent evolution of stellar populations. Adopting a statistical method based on multi-epoch line-of-sight velocity variations, we constrain the binary fraction, $f_b$, of field main-sequence turn-off stars in the Milky Way using data from the second data release of the DESI Milky Way Survey. Our measurements are mainly sensitive to binaries with orbital periods shorter than approximately $10^4$ days. The inferred total binary fractions account statistically for less detectable systems through forward modeling under an assumed orbital-period distribution. $f_b$ is found to primarily increase with lower [Fe/H]. At $[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]\gtrsim -1.3$, $f_b$ shows a modest increase with increasing [Mg/Fe], whereas no clear trend is detected at lower [Fe/H]. The apparent variations of $f_b$ with angular momentum and Galactic height are largely explained by their underlying [Fe/H] distributions, while the remaining variations broadly follow differences in [Mg/Fe]. Within overlapping regions of the [Fe/H]--[Mg/Fe] plane, the thin disk, thick disk, stellar halo and GSE populations exhibit no significant differences in their binary fractions. Thus, our measurements indicate that the variation in $f_b$ is dominated by chemical abundance, which could be explained by the metallicity-dependent gas cooling efficiency and fragmentation. The weaker [Mg/Fe] dependence at fixed [Fe/H] might be associated with the formation conditions of stars, with higher [Mg/Fe] stars generally forming earlier under a more gas-rich and turbulent environment.

papers.title: Prompts versus Rules: Auditing and Controlling Speech Naturalness Behaviors in Voice User Simulators
papers.abstract: As voice agents gain more popularity commercially, the user simulators used to evaluate the deployed agents are also being developed to include more realistic, variable, and diverse speech naturalness behaviors -- disfluency, interruption and backchanneling. The quality of the user simulator directly affects the validity of agent evaluation results. However, we find that most studies so far have not examined in detail whether the intended configuration for these behaviors is realized in the simulation. In this study, we audit the realized naturalness behaviors of tau-Voice, our own LLM-based prompting approach across three models, and our rule-based injection algorithm for disfluency, interruption, and backchanneling. We find that prompting for these behaviors is unreliable and produces speech inconsistent with the instructions, placed and distributed less naturally than the instruction implies. In contrast, our rule-based, model-free algorithm produces controllable and diverse naturalness behaviors more aligned with natural speech. Our results suggest that LLMs not purpose-trained for user simulation are not sufficient on their own to represent authentic user behavior, and that linguistically informed deterministic approaches or specialized models are needed to close the gap; auditing and reporting realized naturalness behaviors, rather than configured settings, is what makes that gap visible.

papers.title: Inter-Categorical Subobject Analysis
papers.abstract: We introduce a systematic way to use the subobject functor on any category to set up a framework for generalized topological and measure-theoretic notions and inferences. Concretely, we develop two connected calculi: 1. a fourfold calculus derived from notions of smallness and density that generalizes, among other things, topological density and measure-theoretic negligibility, 2. a twofold calculus that generalizes topological and measure-theoretic inference procedures. The resulting theory is distinguished in that it is inter-categorical in character: its definitions can be applied not just to describe smallness and density of subobjects in any category and classify morphisms by how they handle them, but also functors and natural transformations by how they transform them, somewhat like the theory of limits but with a simple and intuitive conceptual meaning that applies to each incarnation. We provide examples of these notions from many areas of mathematics and outline their unfolding throughout category theory as we add assumptions that bring them closer to classical settings, which we complete by generalizing the topological duality of open and closed subsets and outlining a possible framework for a categorical measure theory. Central to this interaction is the subobject 2-functor and the 2-category of upward-bounded preorders, so in the last part of the text we provide a study of their function. Concretely we derive representation theorems for this 2-functor and 2-category and a conjecture about how to generalize these theorems to n-categories.

papers.title: Wieszcz-XIX: A 3.1-Billion-Word Corpus of Pre-1918 Polish and Temporally Bounded Language Models Trained From Scratch
papers.abstract: Historical Polish is well documented as a language but annotated in machine-readable form only to about a million words for the period this paper covers; the rest sits behind optical character recognition of variable quality. We present Wieszcz-XIX, a corpus of 6.75 billion tokens (about 3.1 billion words) in 294,369 documents, most of them periodical issues, of Polish published from 1800 to 1918, assembled from Wolne Lektury and the Internet Archive by a pipeline that filters, deduplicates, audits for post-1918 leakage and splits at the document level.
